newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Protests by Zimbabwe veterans hurt Mugabe's image.
newsitem.headline: Protests by Zimbabwe veterans hurt Mugabe's image.

text.p: Violent pay protests by guerrilla war veterans have hurt Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe's image and political analysts say he could be more deeply damaged if the five-month dispute drags on.

In the latest rampage, some of Mugabe's fellow veterans of the battle for independence from Britain looted his ZANU-PF party headquarters on Wednesday night, according to state media, ransacking its offices in the capital Harare, cutting telephone lines, looting food and cigarettes and briefly holding some workers hostage.
Mugabe, 73, is himself a former guerrilla who led the war in what was then Rhodesia and has ruled since independence in 1980.

Even before Wednesday night's fracas, analysts said the president could face more unrest if he let the dispute fester, widening the focus to a host of other problems such as rising unemployment and allegations of corruption.
"The longer it runs...the more damaging it becomes," said John Makumbe, a political scientist at Harare's University of Zimbabwe.

"The logical thing is to pay, and I think he will do just that. That has been his style," he said of demands by the veterans that the government resume unconditionally war victims' compensation suspended in March over charges of widespread fraud.

Makumbe and other analysts charge that Mugabe, sole ruler for the last 17 years, has entrenched himself in power through a political patronage system linked to state coffers, which they say siphons off nearly 40 percent of gross domestic product.
Mugabe says he is "just popular", but he has been fighting a public relations battle since being re-elected 18 months ago to what many of his compatriots believe will be his last six-year term.
He is resolutely defending himself against charges of economic mismanagement and of allowing a scheme meant to support black economic empowerment to enrich only the political elite and their cronies.

But analysts such as Makumbe and Masipula Sithole, also of the University of Zimbabwe, believe the dispute over the war victims' compensation fund is "It creates the impression of social chaos...of a man losing political control. It is bad for investment," said Sithole.
If street protests continued, Sithole said, they could attract an army of unemployed urban youths, notorious for looting property in previous demonstrations.
The ex-guerrilla fighters had solidly backed Mugabe since he led them in the seven-year bush war that culminated in independence.
But he sparked their fury by suspending the multi-million dollar compensation fund after reports that it had been raided by undeserving state officials, including cabinet ministers.
Mugabe has resumed the payments on a slow, case-by-case basis and set up a judicial commission to investigate the fraud charges.

The ex-combatants allege they are being made to suffer for government inefficiency and have in the last two months marched on Mugabe's official residence, held ministers hostage and threatened to lynch some, forcing riot-control police to rescue them.

They have disrupted government-organised functions across the country and last Friday, a mob of ex-fighters stormed a government complex and beat up an official in charge of the war victims' compensation fund.

On Monday they heckled Mugabe during a speech at a Heroes' Day rally in Harare, stealing the limelight before a crowd of about 10,000, including foreign diplomats, and a national audience as the rally was beamed live by state television.
They carried placards calling on Mugabe, patron of the Zimbabwe National War Veterans Association, to come and meet them and branding his government "looters and liars".
Mugabe, who says he will meet them when he has the full facts, looked disturbed but made no reference to the protest.
Some angry officials, including ruling ZANU-PF national chairman Joseph Msika, called it "an act of rebellion and an unacceptable lack of respect for the president".

Other officials, including influential Justice Minister Emmerson Mnangagwa, have been urging the government to keep its focus on the issue, suggesting that it could consider paying every former guerrilla a monthly pension of Z$1,000 (U.S. $85.90).
Some 32,000 guerrillas were in camp when the independence war ended at the end of 1979, but government officials say the badly kept register has ballooned to around 70,000.
The official Herald newspaper urged Mugabe not to succumb to pressure, but said Zimbabwe could be heading for trouble.
"We are headed for difficult times unless these particular ex-combatants reorient," it said in a Wednesday editorial.

Political commentator Lupi Mushayakarara said the veterans enjoyed public support against a government that had failed to meet some key electoral pledges, such as land for peasants, and to tackle unemployment, which has doubled to about 50 percent in a decade.
"The stakes are high in this case and Mugabe just has to swallow his pride instead of risking social trouble," she told Reuters.
($1 = $11.645 Zimbabwe Dollars)
